analysis.one_liner: Would have required emergency federal safety rules to protect coal miners from COVID-19 exposure.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan sponsorship from both of West Virginia's senators, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate committee it was sent to.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Labor Department to issue, within a week of passage, emergency rules requiring mine operators to give miners protective equipment against COVID-19. It would have barred operators from punishing miners who report hazards or wear their own better masks, and required tracking of COVID-19 infections among miners. It also called for permanent infection-control standards for mines within two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal and other miners, who work underground and in confined spaces in close quarters, would have gained enforceable protections: mandatory personal protective equipment supplied by operators, protection from being fired or disciplined for raising safety concerns or wearing higher-grade masks, and government tracking of how COVID-19 spread through mining workforces.

how_it_helps.text: The Labor Department would have had to issue an emergency temporary standard within 7 days of enactment, requiring mine operators to provide personal protective equipment and supplies to reduce miners' exposure to SARS-CoV-2.

The standards would have prohibited operators from discriminating or retaliating against miners for reporting violations, raising good-faith concerns about infectious-disease hazards, or voluntarily using protective equipment better than what the operator supplied.
Labor would have collected and analyzed case data, investigated individual COVID-19 cases among miners, published regular public reports, and made recommendations to protect miners.

The bill required a permanent standard within 24 months to protect miners from occupational exposure to infectious pathogens, including novel ones, enforceable like any standard under the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act.

analysis.who_pays: Mine operators, who would bear the cost of supplying protective equipment and supplies, recording and reporting work-related infections, and complying with new infection-control rules — and who would face enforcement if they retaliated against workers who spoke up.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have imposed new equipment, recordkeeping, and reporting costs on mine operators during a pandemic that was already disrupting coal production and demand.

To move fast, the bill waived normal rulemaking checks for the emergency standard, including the Regulatory Flexibility Act, the Paperwork Reduction Act, the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, and Executive Order 12866 review — meaning no small-business impact analysis or cost-benefit review before the rules took effect.

The emergency standard would have remained in force indefinitely until a final standard took effect, extending beyond the standard limits in the Mine Safety and Health Act's emergency-rulemaking process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For miners, the benefit was direct protection from a serious workplace hazard in confined, close-quarters work, plus protection against retaliation for reporting it. The main cost fell on operators, mostly equipment and recordkeeping, and the bill traded away some normal regulatory review to move quickly. The tradeoff favored workers' safety, which is one reason the fast-track process drew the objection it did.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Joe Manchin introduced the bill on May 13, 2020, joined by seven cosponsors from both parties, including Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, the other senator from West Virginia.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or vote — appears in the record for the rest of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mine operators avoided the mandated emergency protective-equipment standard and its compliance costs, while miners did not get the federal COVID-19 protections the bill would have required.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's Republican cosponsor.

for.name: 6 of 8 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Durbin, Kaine, Jones, Brown, Casey, Warner).

against.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; it stayed at referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — 6 Democrats and 1 Republican among 7 cosponsors, including both of West Virginia's senators — so its death in committee was not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required operators to buy and supply protective equipment, record and report work-related COVID-19 cases, and adopt anti-retaliation policies — costs and legal exposure they avoid with the bill dead. Miners work in confined underground spaces where the industry's cost of protection is the workers' safety, so the operators' interest in blocking the mandate ran against the workers' interest.
